title: Camel Case Conversion: Casing Rules and Width Pitfalls
description: How one regex produces camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, kebab-case, and CONSTANT_CASE, plus acronym, digit, Chinese, punctuation, and width edge cases.
content:
The usual way to convert to camel case is to split the text into words first and then join them according to the target rule. For example, user_name, user-name, and user name all yield userName. The text-transform tool on this site works exactly that way: the first word stays lowercase and each following word is capitalized. The real trouble spots are consecutive uppercase acronyms, Chinese, and full-width characters, not the joining step.

How the tool splits words: one regex decides every result

camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, kebab-case, and CONSTANT_CASE all share the same splitWords. It calls trim() on the input, splits with /[\s_\-]+|(?=[A-Z])/, lowercases each word, and finally filters out empty strings. In other words, there are only three kinds of separators: any whitespace, underscores, and hyphens, plus the zero-width position before each ASCII uppercase letter.

  • Whitespace: spaces, tabs, and newlines all count, and the full-width space U+3000 also falls under \s.
  • Underscores and hyphens: several in a row are treated as a single separator.
  • ASCII uppercase letters: (?=[A-Z]) splits without consuming a character, so userName becomes user and name.
  • Other characters do not split: commas, periods, parentheses, Chinese, and emoji all stay inside the word they belong to.
function splitWords(s) {
  return s
    .trim()
    .split(/[\s_\-]+|(?=[A-Z])/)
    .map((w) => w.toLowerCase())
    .filter(Boolean);
}

Because every word is passed through toLowerCase(), the original casing information is lost during splitting. That also explains why converting userName to camelCase again still gives userName, while HTTPServer turns into a string of single letters.

camelCase and PascalCase: the first word and single-letter words

camelCase keeps the first word lowercase, then capitalizes the first character of each following word and joins them; PascalCase capitalizes the first letter of every word. The implementation uses w[0].toUpperCase() + w.slice(1) rather than "capitalize the whole word and leave the rest unchanged", so every word is already lowercase before this step.

case 'camel':
  return words.map((w, i) => (i === 0 ? w : w[0].toUpperCase() + w.slice(1))).join('');
case 'pascal':
  return words.map((w) => w[0].toUpperCase() + w.slice(1)).join('');

The camelCase of HTTPServer is not the familiar httpServer but hTTPServer: the H, T, T, and P of the acronym each become a word, and each is capitalized again when joined. Conversely, the PascalCase of HTTPServer happens to equal the original, because every single-letter word is restored to uppercase. Single-letter words are the most easily overlooked input for this rule set.

snake_case, kebab-case, and CONSTANT_CASE

These three modes only change the connector: snake_case joins with underscores, kebab-case joins with hyphens, and CONSTANT_CASE joins with underscores and then uppercases the whole string. Each converted word is already lowercase, so the "all uppercase" step of CONSTANT_CASE actually applies to the joined result, and punctuation and non-ASCII characters also go through toUpperCase().

Note that the space in the "Full-width" row is still an ordinary space, U+0020, not the full-width space U+3000. That is not a typesetting oversight: the character-by-character mapping covers only ASCII ! through ~. For the same reason, when full-width input is converted to half-width, U+3000 does not become an ordinary space.

title and sentence only touch ASCII word starts

"Title case" uses src.replace(/\b\w/g, ...). In non-Unicode mode, \w is equivalent to [A-Za-z0-9_], and \b also decides boundaries by that ASCII word-character set. It therefore only uppercases basic Latin letters; Chinese, full-width letters, and emoji are never treated as the start of a word. Accented letters are outside \w as well, so éclair becomes éClair, not Éclair.

This mode only uppercases; it does not lowercase the remaining letters. hELLO wORLD becomes HELLO WORLD, and eBay becomes EBay. The apostrophe is another trap: the t in don't is preceded by a non-word character, which forms a new word boundary, so title gives Don'T. Underscores are the opposite: foo_bar is capitalized only at the start, giving Foo_bar.

"Sentence case" uses /(^\s*\w|[.!?。！？]\s*\w)/g and covers only three positions: the start of the string, after a half-width period/exclamation mark/question mark, and after a Chinese period/exclamation mark/question mark. It also recognizes only the ASCII \w, so the Chinese string 中文。下一句 is unchanged, while 中文。hello becomes 中文。Hello; if the text starts with Chinese, ^\s*\w also fails to match the English word that follows. Unlike title, sentence does not touch the letter after an apostrophe, and don't stays Don't.

Both modes preserve existing whitespace and punctuation, do no trimming, and leave unmatched casing unchanged. That means they suit display-level capitalization, not normalizing arbitrary text into a naming convention.

Full-width conversion: add 0xFEE0, leave spaces alone

The regex for "to full-width" is /[!-~]/g, which matches the visible ASCII characters U+0021 through U+007E and then adds 0xFEE0 to the code point, producing the full-width forms U+FF01–U+FF5E. Letters, digits, underscores, and punctuation are all in range; the space U+0020 is not, so the output of Hello, World! is Ｈｅｌｌｏ， Ｗｏｒｌｄ！, with an ordinary space still between the two words.

src.replace(/[!-~]/g, (c) =>
  String.fromCharCode(c.charCodeAt(0) + 0xfee0));

This rule also explains why user_name becomes ｕｓｅｒ＿ｎａｍｅ: the underscore is a visible ASCII character and turns into a full-width underscore too. Conversely, Chinese, emoji, and characters that are already full-width are outside [!-~] and are kept as-is. The full-width mode is not "turn the whole text into full-width typography" but "replace visible ASCII characters with their full-width compatibility equivalents".

Half-width conversion: subtract 0xFEE0, keep U+3000 and half-width kana

"To half-width" matches only [\uFF01-\uFF5E] and subtracts 0xFEE0. Together with the full-width mode it forms a pair of inverse mappings, but the coverage is limited to this block of compatibility characters. The full-width space U+3000 is outside the range, half-width katakana U+FF61–U+FF9F are outside the range, and the Chinese punctuation U+3002 and U+3001 are outside as well. Thus Ｈｅｌｌｏ，　Ｗｏｒｌｄ！ becomes Hello,　World!, still with U+3000 in the middle; for 。、！？ only the last two punctuation marks become half-width.

src.replace(/[\uFF01-\uFF5E]/g, (c) =>
  String.fromCharCode(c.charCodeAt(0) - 0xfee0));

So "to half-width" cannot be treated as general width normalization. Unicode NFKC performs compatibility decomposition and folds half-width and full-width katakana, full-width ASCII, and other compatibility forms into the same string, but this tool only adds or subtracts the code points in the block above. When strict normalization is needed, use normalize('NFKC') and handle the other compatibility folds it introduces separately, rather than expecting this button to do the whole job.

What happens to digits, punctuation, Chinese, and newlines

Digits are not word boundaries. v2 is always a single word; v2 API gives camelCase v2API and snake_case v2_a_p_i; user2FA splits only before F and A, giving user2_f_a, while all-lowercase user2fa is not split at all. The boundary between a digit and a letter depends on whether the ASCII letter is uppercase (non-ASCII uppercase letters do not trigger a split).

Punctuation is not a separator either. The first word of hello, world is hello,, so snake_case gives hello,_world and camelCase gives hello,World; a.b is a single word, and all five naming modes keep the period. Only whitespace, underscores, and hyphens are consumed.

Chinese has no case and does not trigger the (?=[A-Z]) split, so 用户Name gives two words, 用户 and name, and snake_case outputs 用户_name. Emoji likewise trigger no split and are not rewritten by any mode; they stick to the adjacent word, so for example good followed directly by an emoji is still one word. When you need to split on emoji or Chinese words, this tool does not provide those boundaries.

In camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, kebab-case, and CONSTANT_CASE, newlines are whitespace separators, and multi-line text is joined into one continuous string (kebab-case yields names like a-b, which not every language treats as a valid identifier). In the all-uppercase, all-lowercase, title, sentence, and width modes, newlines are preserved as-is. The difference comes from the former modes all calling splitWords, while the latter replace directly on the original string.

Boundaries and limitations

To sum up the behavior above, confirm at least the following before you use it.

  • Acronyms are split into single letters. HTTPServer in snake_case is h_t_t_p_server, XMLHttpRequest in camelCase is xMLHttpRequest, and userID in snake_case is user_i_d. The tool has no acronym dictionary and does not recognize consecutive uppercase letters as one word.
  • title and sentence only understand ASCII. \w is [A-Za-z0-9_], so Chinese, full-width letters, and accented letters are not word characters; the apostrophe counts as a boundary, so title turns don't into Don'T, while sentence capitalizes only the leading d and leaves the t after the apostrophe lowercase, giving Don't.
  • Full-width conversion excludes spaces. It handles only U+0021–U+007E, and an ordinary space stays U+0020; half-width conversion handles only U+FF01–U+FF5E and does not touch U+3000, half-width katakana, or Chinese punctuation.
  • Digits, Chinese, and emoji provide no boundaries. user2fa is not split into user and 2fa; Chinese is split only at whitespace, underscores, hyphens, or ASCII uppercase letters, and emoji stay inside the word; punctuation is not stripped either.
  • trim timing is inconsistent. The five naming modes trim before splitting; the all-uppercase, all-lowercase, title, sentence, and width modes preserve leading and trailing whitespace. If the input is only spaces or pure underscores, the naming modes output an empty string, but the UI still says "conversion complete", because the empty-value check only looks at whether the raw input is an empty string.
  • Case mapping can change length. ß uppercases to SS, and lowercasing some accented letters splits them into multiple code points; if a downstream system truncates by character count, it must work by code point rather than UTF-16 unit.

These limitations do not make the tool unusable; they show that it performs "mechanical conversion based on separators and ASCII casing". Variable names, configuration keys, and file names are good candidates to start with it; title typography, linguistically meaningful word-initial capitalization, and Unicode width normalization are outside its scope.

Choose a mode for the target convention and review

Decide on the target convention first, then how to prepare the input. When you need to turn a multi-line list into one value per line, you can first use the text toolbox to deduplicate and drop blank lines; to check whether the word-splitting regex behaves as expected, try the same expressions section by section in the regex tester. If naming results will go into a URL path or query parameter, encode them separately in the URL encoder; do not assume the naming conversion has already handled escaping.

  1. Confirm the target: camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, kebab-case, or CONSTANT_CASE, and avoid mixing them in one project.
  2. Handle acronyms first: rewrite a run of capitals such as HTTPServer into a form the tool recognizes, or fix the single-letter segments by hand after conversion.
  3. Check digits and punctuation: make sure v2, user2fa, and phrases with commas were not split into unexpected words.
  4. Split multi-line input first: the naming modes treat newlines as separators, so process line by line to get one identifier per line.
  5. Check the width modes separately: check whether spaces are still U+0020, whether U+3000 remains, and whether half-width kana need separate handling.

Finally, do a reverse check: paste the result back into the tool and convert with the opposite mode to see whether you return to the expected word sequence. A mismatch on the round trip is usually not a tool bug; the original text already contained acronyms, punctuation, or full-width spaces, and that information was lost in the first conversion.

faqs.q: Why does HTTPServer become h_t_t_p_server in snake_case?
faqs.a: splitWords splits before every ASCII uppercase letter, so the consecutive capitals H, T, T, and P each become a word; they are then lowercased and joined with underscores. The tool has no acronym dictionary; write it as HttpServer first, or merge the single-letter segments by hand after conversion.

faqs.q: What does userName become in kebab-case?
faqs.a: It becomes user-name. The split happens before the uppercase N, giving the two words user and name, which are then joined with a hyphen. Likewise, userName in snake_case is user_name.

faqs.q: Why doesn't full-width to half-width handle the full-width space and half-width kana?
faqs.a: The half-width mode matches only U+FF01–U+FF5E and subtracts 0xFEE0. The full-width space U+3000 and half-width katakana U+FF61–U+FF9F are outside this range, as are the Chinese punctuation marks U+3002 and U+3001. Use Unicode NFKC for broader compatibility normalization, or replace those characters separately.

faqs.q: Why does multi-line text become one line in camelCase?
faqs.a: The naming modes all call splitWords, and newlines count as whitespace separators, so all words are split and then joined with an empty string. To preserve line structure, first split the text by line in a text-processing tool and convert each line, or use modes such as all-uppercase and all-lowercase that operate directly on the original string.

faqs.q: Why does title mode turn don't into Don'T?
faqs.a: title uses /\b\w/g, and \w covers ASCII letters, digits, and underscores; the apostrophe is not a word character, so the t after it is treated as a new word boundary and uppercased. sentence mode handles only the start of the sentence and the characters after punctuation, so in don't only the leading d is capitalized and the t after the apostrophe stays lowercase, giving Don't.

focus: Split words first, then join; acronyms, digits, Chinese, and full-width spaces decide whether the output matches expectations.
notice: Conversion runs locally in your browser; text is never uploaded. Results follow character rules only, with no tokenization or semantic analysis, so review important identifiers manually.
